title: What's new in Pyroscope: profile more of your workflows, troubleshoot with AI agents, and more
description:
When an application slows down or memory usage keeps climbing, knowing which code is responsible can help you find a fix faster. Continuous profiling gives you that visibility, so you can see where your application spends resources such as CPU time and memory.We’ve made updates to Pyroscope, our open source continuous profiling database, that make it easier to profile your applications, find performance bottlenecks, and optimize your code, whether you're doing the work yourself or with an AI agent. Highlights include:Profile more of your workloads: Memory profiling for Python and Rust, and .NET support on Windows, helps you find performance bottlenecks across more of your services.Let AI agents work with your profiling data: Pyroscope commands in gcx, the Grafana CLI, let an agent query your profiles directly.See more of your profiling data in Grafana: Exemplars and a new Call Tree view help you explore your profiles visually, whether you're investigating on your own or looking at what an agent found.Many of these capabilities build directly on Pyroscope 2.0, the ground-up rearchitecture of Pyroscope that makes continuous profiling more cost-effective at scale (in our production environment, it reduced the symbol storage footprint by up to 95%). For example, exemplars require the v2 storage layer that Pyroscope 2.0 is built on. Read on to learn more about some of the latest updates. And for a full list of recent changes, see the release notes for Pyroscope and Profiles Drilldown.Profile more of your workloadsMemory profiling and Windows support have been some of the most frequently requested features for Pyroscope. If you run Python or Rust services, you can now use the Pyroscope SDKs to see where their memory goes, not just their CPU time. If you run .NET applications on Windows, you can now profile those, too.Find memory leaks and heavy allocation: memory profiling for PythonMemory issues can be hard to track down from metrics alone. A container's memory graph shows that usage is climbing, but not which code is allocating that memory. CPU profiles don't answer that either, since they show where your code spends time. Memory profiles show which code paths allocate the most memory and which allocated the memory that's still in use, which is what you need when a service's memory keeps growing, or its allocations drive up garbage collection work.The Python SDK now supports memory profiling, so you can see which code allocates the most memory and which code allocated the memory that's still in use, alongside the CPU profiles you already collect. Enable it with mem_enabled=True:pyroscope.configure(
    application_name = "my.python.app",
    server_address   = "http://my-pyroscope-server:4040",
    mem_enabled      = True,
)
To learn more, see the PR and the Python SDK docs.Find memory leaks and heap growth: memory profiling for RustIn addition to CPU profiling, the Pyroscope Rust SDK now supports memory profiling through the jemalloc allocator. It reports in-use memory, so you can see which code paths allocated the most live memory and track down heap growth and leaks.To learn more, see the PR, the Rust SDK docs, and the jemalloc example.Profile .NET applications on Windows If you run .NET applications on Windows, including .NET Framework applications hosted in IIS, you can now send profiles from them to Pyroscope and find hot spots without migrating them first. Windows support is for x64, starting with version 1.3.0 of the profiler. On .NET 8, 9, and 10, you get the same profile types on Windows as on Linux, enabled with the same environment variables. On .NET Framework 4.7 and later, CPU and wall-time profiling are available.To learn more, see the PR and the .NET SDK docs. Note: this feature is currently in public preview. Let AI agents work with your profiling dataWithout access to your profiles, an AI coding agent can only reason about why a service is slow from the code in front of it, or you have to copy flame graphs and numbers into the conversation by hand. With access to your profiles, it can work from the same data you would, with visibility into which services use the most resources, which functions are responsible, and what a specific profile looked like at a specific time.gcx, the Grafana CLI, gives you and your AI coding agent structured access to your Grafana instance, from dashboards and alerts to metrics, logs, traces, and profiles. gcx enables agent mode automatically in many coding agents, such as Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor, and you can enable it yourself for any other agent with --agent. gcx now also includes gcx profiles commands for querying Pyroscope. To see gcx in action with Pyroscope, both in the terminal and with an AI agent, watch this community call.Below are some of the ways you can use gcx with your profiling data, whether you run the commands yourself or an agent runs them for you. You don't need to run your own stack to try them. Grafana Play has demo data you can query, so you can point gcx at it by adding a play context:gcx config set stacks.play.grafana.server https://play.grafana.org
gcx config set stacks.play.grafana.org-id 1
gcx config set contexts.play.stack play
export GCX_CONTEXT=playGCX_CONTEXT selects the play context for commands in this terminal session, without changing your default context. The commands below also use the Play profiles data source, grafanacloud-profiles. To use your own data, open a new terminal, leave out -d grafanacloud-profiles, and change the service name.Start with the services using the most resourcesWhen you run many services, it's not always clear which one to look at first. gcx profiles metrics --top ranks your services by a profile type, such as CPU, over a time window, so you or your agent can start with the ones using the most resources:gcx profiles metrics '{}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h \
  --top
To try this with your AI coding agent and the Grafana Play data, use this prompt:Using gcx with the play context, find which services used the most CPU over the last hour in the grafanacloud-profiles datasource.
To learn more, see the PR and the gcx profiles metrics CLI reference docs.Go from the combined view to the exact profile with exemplarsAn aggregated profile blends every instance of a service together over the time range, so a single misbehaving process can be hard to spot. Exemplars show individual profiles ranked by their value for the profile type you query, such as CPU time or memory, so you or your agent can go straight to the most expensive ones and see what happened in each, instead of only the combined total.gcx profiles exemplars lists the most expensive individual profiles, and you can pass one of their profile IDs to gcx profiles query to see the top functions in just that profile:gcx profiles exemplars profile '{service_name="checkoutservice"}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h
gcx profiles query '{service_name="checkoutservice"}' \
  -d grafanacloud-profiles \
  --profile-type process_cpu:cpu:nanoseconds:cpu:nanoseconds \
  --since 1h \
  --profile-id <PROFILE_ID>If your profiles are linked to traces, you can also narrow a query to a single span or trace to see the code that ran during a slow operation or request.To try this with your AI coding agent and the Grafana Play data, use this prompt:Use exemplars to find the most expensive CPU profile for checkoutservice in the grafanacloud-profiles datasource in the last hour, and summarize its most CPU-intensive functions.
To learn more, see the PRs for exemplars, profile IDs, and span and trace selectors. Also see the exemplars CLI reference docs and query CLI reference docs.Export profiles to use with other toolsSometimes you want the raw profile: to open it in tools you already use, to attach it to an issue, or to keep a snapshot from before a change so you can compare later. Add -o pprof to gcx profiles query to download the profile as a pprof file, which you can open with go tool pprof.You can also start from the Grafana UI. With the release of Profiles Drilldown 3.0 in October, you can click the Export profile data download icon above the flame graph and select gcx command, which copies a gcx profiles query command that downloads the profile you're looking at as a pprof file. In the diff flame graph view, gcx commands copies two commands, one for the baseline profile and one for the comparison.To learn more, see the PRs for -o pprof and copying gcx commands, the Export profile data in the Profiles Drilldown docs, and the gcx profiles query CLI reference docs.See more of your profiling data in GrafanaThe Grafana UI now includes exemplars to look at one profile at a time, and the Call Tree, to follow exactly how your code reached an expensive function. Use them on your own, or to look at what an agent found and see the same data for yourself.See one profile at a time with exemplarsThe same individual profiles that gcx profiles exemplars returns are also in the Grafana UI. When you're looking at a spike, exemplars let you see the individual profiles from single processes at that moment, instead of only the combined total for the whole time range. Exemplars show up as markers on the time series, plotted at each profile's value. In Profiles Drilldown, they're on by default in the Flame graph and Labels views, and you can turn them on in other views. Click a marker to see its labels, such as the host or, if you run on Kubernetes, the pod and namespace. Then select View profile to see the flame graph for just the profile. In Explore, turn on Exemplars under the Pyroscope query's Options.To learn more, see our docs on exemplars concepts, drilling down to an individual profile, and available views, as well as this community call.Follow call paths with the Call Tree viewFlame graphs and the top table are good at showing where resources are spent, but in deep or wide stacks, it can be hard to follow the exact path your code took to reach an expensive function. The new Call Tree view shows the same data as an expandable tree, so you can follow that path one call at a time. It's available in Profiles Drilldown 2.3.0 and later, in Explore, and in the flame graph panel starting in Grafana 13.3. On earlier Grafana versions, enable the flameGraphWithCallTree feature toggle.When an expensive function, such as a serialization or logging call, is called from many places, use Show callers to see every path that leads to it and which caller matters most. You can also show the Call Tree side by side with a flame graph, and both stay in sync as you focus on a function.To learn more, see the PR, the call tree mode docs, and the August community call.How to learn moreTo see the full list of recent improvements and fixes, please refer to the release notes for Pyroscope and Profiles Drilldown, and the gcx repository.If you are interested in hearing more about Pyroscope news, please join us on the Grafana Labs Community Slack or start a conversation in GitHub Discussions. We'd love to hear what you think.

title: An early look at the Grafana UI refresh: Building a clearer, more consistent user experience
description: Whether you’re investigating an incident or just exploring your data, a clear, consistent UI helps you move between workflows and find what matters faster. As Grafana has grown to support more use cases, we’ve seen opportunities to improve on that experience. That’s why, as part of the Grafana 13.3 release, we introduced the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7.We’re approaching this work in phases, with the refreshed UI currently in public preview in both Grafana Cloud and self-managed versions of Grafana, and your feedback will play a major role in shaping what comes next. In this post, we’ll give you a closer look at why we decided to make this change now, why we think visual aesthetics matter in a UI, and the impact this will have on the Grafana user experience. You can also check out some of the visual updates in the video below.Starting with why“Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.” – Donella MeadowsAt Grafana Labs, our culture empowers individuals and teams to identify user needs, build solutions quickly, ship iteratively, and work in the open. This has allowed us to cover a large range of use cases with Grafana. But moving fast can come with challenges, including design debt, which leads to inconsistent and sometimes conflicting visual cues, workflows, and GUIs. We were aware of these challenges, but our focus remained steadfast on providing new functionality and supporting as many use cases as possible.Meanwhile, over the last year, the product design team has worked with our engineers to build new interaction patterns to support AI solutions like Grafana Assistant and Assistant Workspace. Building these patterns opened the door to curiosity, and we started experimenting with new visual forms, colors, shapes, and effects that laid the groundwork for the refresh.Through this work, our approach to UI style and aesthetics evolved, and so did our purpose: alongside supporting new workflows and use cases, we wanted to bring greater consistency to interactions and design patterns across Grafana. This refresh is the first step toward that goal.Visual styling and usability“The aesthetic quality of a product is integral to its usefulness.” – Dieter RamsSo why invest in visual styling? To stay relevant? To facilitate sales conversations? Because it looks cool?All of those reasons are valid, but at Grafana Labs, product designers are utilitarians first. We believe digital products should exist with a clear purpose and function in mind. We think each color, font style, and line should establish a clear information hierarchy and help users quickly understand what's on the page, ultimately making our product easier to use.As more workflows shift to terminals and agentic chat interfaces, we believe investing in visual style now is foundational to Grafana’s future usability. When fewer user journeys rely on a traditional UI, those that do must emphasize clarity and consistency.What’s new: a closer look This first phase of the refresh focuses on making the Grafana UI clearer and more consistent across workflows and components, while giving you time to adapt to the changes. Here are some of the highlights:New default light and dark themes: These themes use completely new color palettes with improved accessibility compliance by design.Increased consistency across components: We have started to reduce the amount of available UI components and their variants. This means users only need to learn an interaction or a pattern once, and can then leverage it across the entire platform.New font styles, borders, and shadows: By overhauling our visual primitives to work in a proportional and scalable way, we create layers of hierarchy and visual information. As part of our audits, we noticed that many areas of the UI competed for users’ attention. We’re moving to a state where you can immediately understand what’s most important on a page, so you can complete tasks faster and more efficiently. You’ll notice these changes across the building blocks of Grafana, including cards, panels, and drawers.We’re rolling out the visual refresh gradually so Grafana contributors and users have time to adapt without disrupting critical workflows. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Existing navigation stays the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous styling at any time.For a full list of changes in the public preview, please visit our documentation.Curiosity, monitoring, and feedback"There are three key practices needed in order to build and maintain a circle of competence: curiosity and a desire to learn, monitoring, and feedback." – Shane Parrish & Rhiannon BeaubienCuriosity is a key attribute of product designers at Grafana Labs and we knew that unifying the look and feel across Grafana meant making choices that could elicit strong reactions. This is why learning, gathering feedback, and monitoring the response have been central to our process.We could have spent a year working on what we think is a perfect new visual styling, running hundreds of internal iterations, but instead we started with early internal dogfooding of the refreshed UI. This led to honest discussions and opinions from Grafanistas across the company, helping us iterate the visual refresh rapidly into a version we could not have achieved without working openly. Now, with the refresh in public preview, your feedback is central to how we’ll continue to refine our visual styling. Through our community Slack and a temporary in-app survey, you can tell us directly what’s working, what needs improvement, and what we might have missed. We monitor and discuss this feedback in the open, helping to amplify your voice and share it across the organization. Your responses will be integral to shaping future iterations of the refresh.We can’t wait to hear what you think, and to continue our evolution toward a bolder visual experience for all Grafana users.

title: Bliki: Generated Glossary
description:
When we use LLMs in a specialized domain, such as the operations of any
  reasonably-large organization, there is a lot of specialized vocabulary. Such
  words and specialized meanings will be foreign to an LLM because they aren't
  in its training set, making it harder for the LLM to be effective when doing
  tasks in that domain. One technique to aid this is to use an LLM to generate a
  glossary of the terminology in that domain, and make this glossary available
  for any LLMs doing work in those circumstances.

The sources for the LLM can be any material within the organization
  concerned such as documents, emails, and chat logs. In some cases getting
  transcripts of audio or video may be helpful, although most organizations
  generate enough text to do the job.

The glossary-generating LLM should look for single words, and phrases of
  several words that regularly hang out together to form a meaningful term. The
  generator should be asked to identify terms that are new to it, but also known
  terms that are being used in unfamiliar ways. The latter can often cause the
  most confusion.

Once we have a list of specialized vocabulary we can ask the agent to
  produce a glossary, with definitions for each term. Some terms may
  be used in different ways, in which case the LLM should provide alternative
  definitions, with a note as to what context the differences appear in. The LLM
  can be asked to follow the output format of a dictionary, with a focus on
  precision and conciseness.

Once we have a draft glossary, then  human experts in that domain should
  review it, and amend it for cases where the LLM has got the wrong ends of
  sticks.

We then put the glossary somewhere where any other LLM can use it. It
  should be in a form that's easy for the LLM to consult, and minimize the
  tokens the LLM should consume in order to find meaning. We should set up a
  schedule to review and refresh the glossary at regular intervals, by agents
  and humans. We should keep it in version control, so we can see how it changes
  over time.

Large organizations often have subtly different definitions in different
  places, essentially following the Domain Driven Design notion
  of Bounded Context. Source code can be a particularly
  interesting bounded context, allowing folks to understand how terminology is
  used within a code base. Sometimes a single glossary can span several of
  bounded contexts, but at other times it's better to have separate glossaries
  for each one, allowing LLMs to consult whichever glossaries that are relevant
  to what they are doing. I'd urge everyone to resist any temptation to create a
  single, standard, glossary - I've yet to see that work. Often the value of a
  glossary isn't to nail down a single definition of a term, but instead to
  highlight its different usage in different contexts.

When there are different bounded contexts it can be interesting to compare
  different glossaries, or to get LLMs to compare glossaries and describe
  differences in usage. Comparing a source-code derived glossary to a human text
  can be particularly instructive.

If the glossary is large, it can be worthwhile to only include the terms
  and links to definitions as part of the initial context. The model can then
  use the links for only the full definitions it needs while working.

A glossary can be used in several ways within Agentic Engineering. Glossaries can inform generation of code, so that
  names within the generated software fit the particular vocabulary of the
  enterprise. Sensors in a
  harness can check for this usage, both in the internals of the software
  and in the user-interface.

When generating code or documents, we may introduce new bounded contexts.
  For example, internal names that may be used within an organization should not
  be exposed in a customer-facing UI, because such internal terms are likely to be
  only confuse a customer. In this case a customer has a different bounded
  context to the part of the enterprise serving them.

It's often useful for glossaries to include terms that should not be used,
  in which case it includes advice on what other term to use instead. Terms that
  are deprecated can be handled in this way, with glossary entries that indicate
  what period of time a term should be in effect.

In my conversations with people working with agents in large organizations,
  a common theme is the difficulty of specialized language. This encourages the
  activities of domain modeling, building ontologies, and constructing explicit
  context
  layers in enterprise data. Getting LLMs to generate a glossary is a
  simple, but useful, part of this work.

description:
Automated testing in the age of AI coding assistants is problematic:
     when AI agents write both production and test code, developers risk losing
     the assurance that automated tests protect against functional errors.
     Matteo Vaccari makes three claims: (1) when AI writes the
     code, developers become its customers; (2) therefore customer tests, not
     developer tests, become the primary contract between humans and AI; (3)
     moving that contract into test data rather than test code makes it easier
     to protect it from unexpected modifications by coding agents. All of this
     optimizes for human-readable tests that establish a contract between humans
     and AI. While in the past DSL parsers and custom test runners were

title: Deprecating the Collector Batch Processor
description:
Batching in the OpenTelemetry Collector is a process that ensures requests
are the right size for the exporter, large enough to improve compression and
amortize round-trip latency, but not so large as to exceed limits. Batching
combines a number of concerns that are critical to performance, reliability, and
cost in running Collectors.
Since OpenTelemetry began in 2019, its Collector has included a batch
processor component, responsible for combining and splitting requests before
sending them to downstream consumers, monitoring inbound and outbound timeouts,
and holding back new requests when the pipeline is full.

title: Fragments: November 10
description:
It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar.

The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends.


  One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent.

  Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on?


Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on  the recent election’s impact on data centers.


  I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite.


He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI:


  you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race.


There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition.

He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming.

There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments.

To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse. He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering, in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is.


  I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data?


His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.)

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming.


  Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.


While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains (“I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights.

Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone, by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Jessica Kerr (jessitron):


  My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered.

  Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun.


 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents.


  An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do.


They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context, which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at:


  Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended?
  Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done?
  Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true?
  Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters?
  Security: Should the agent have this context at all?


They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor)

I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords.

 ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄                ❄

Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around:


  What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use.

  70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them.


That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

title: Long-horizon agents and durable execution
description:
Long-horizon agents can automate complex tasks that take days or weeks
     to complete and involve multiple exchanges with people and external
     systems. Many things can go wrong during this time, including process
     crashes, network failures, and unanticipated real-world behavior.
     Kiran Prakash explains durable execution: an emerging
     pattern that helps agents recover from these failures and move towards
     their goal. In this programming model, the runtime keeps a record of the
     result of each step that interacts with the outside world so that, when a
     failure occurs, the program runs again, completed steps are skipped, and
     the program's state is rebuilt from the record.

title: Run cost-effective, always-on agents to monitor your environment: the engineering behind Watchers
description: Alert rules are great for the failures you can predict, but they fall short on the ones you can't. With the advent of modern AI, you might think the solution is to swarm your stack with agents that monitor every last detail, but that can quickly lead to astronomical bills.And those are the gaps Watchers fill: catching what alerts miss while keeping costs in control. Generally Available as of ObservabilityCON 2026, Watchers are always-on agents in Grafana Assistant. You describe what to monitor (in natural language) and pick your data sources, and the watcher learns what "normal" looks like and tells you when you drift from that state. Ultimately, this helps you surface problems without needing an alert, giving you wider coverage and more confidence in your system. But how do we keep Watchers cost-effective for our customers, especially in comparison to building your own agent that runn around the clock? For example, let's say you deploy your own version of a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes, which means it runs 4,320 times a month. If each run were an agentic investigation, which cost us between $0.56 and $1.26 in a recent experiment, that one watcher you built would cost thousands of dollars a month.Yet the Watchers running on our own Grafana Cloud stack cost a median of less than $5 a month. In this post, I'll show you the engineering behind that number, which mostly comes down to one question: where do you actually need an LLM's intelligence, and how much of it?The TL;DR on WatchersWatchers keeps an eye on one things you care about, such as a service, a dependency, or a fix you shipped after an incident. Think of it as the dashboard check you'd otherwise do by hand, done around the clock. It stays quiet until something needs attention, then it sends you its assessment and the evidence behind it. For critical findings, it can also launch an Investigation in Assistant to find the cause.Here's the gist of how it helps you identify potential issues in a cost-effective manner, which I'll cover in greater detail in the remaining sections in this post:The design: A capable agent calibrates each watcher once, so every run after that is plain code plus one call to a small, fast model.The cost: Less than $10 a month per watcher for 41 of our 43 internal Watchers. Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026, and then will bill as part of Assistant token usage.The results: Coverage beyond your alerts, so you catch what you didn’t know to watch for and better trust your system. Our own watcher found more than 10 customer-affecting production bugs in the past few months.The integrations: Watchers read most of your telemetry, plus any HTTP API, and send findings to Slack, Microsoft Teams, webhooks, or Grafana Alerting.Put the intelligence only where it's neededKeeping an eye on a service comes down to three jobs: Working out what to watch and what normal looks likeComparing the same signals with normal again and againDeciding whether anything is worth interrupting someone forOnly the first and last jobs need intelligence, and they need it in very different amounts. Let's go back to our example from the intro about a watcher that checks in every 10 minutes. Determining what to watch takes exploration and judgment, but once you've made a decision, you don't need to revisit it constantly. After all, the answer barely changes between 9 and 9:10 a.m. And deciding whether something matters enough to interrupt someone takes judgment on every run, but it's a narrow question once the legwork is done. The middle job is fetching data and doing arithmetic, which code does well and LLMs don't. So a watcher splits the work three ways:JobWho does itWhenDecide what to watch and what normal looks likeA calibration agent, with a capable model and toolsOnce, and again when you recalibrateFetch the data and compare it with the baselinePlain code: queries, statistics, and log pattern trackingEvery runDecide whether it matters, and explain whyA small, fast model, in a single call with no toolsEvery runAnd here's what that workflow looks like:Calibration: do the hard thinking onceCalibration is the secret sauce. Think of it as pre-processing: when you create a watcher, a background agent does the setup work an experienced engineer would normally do and writes down what it learns. The expensive reasoning happens once, and every run inherits a narrow, well-prepared task that an LLM is good at.The calibration agent:Settles the scope. It maps where your telemetry lives and asks you up front when it hits a question that only you can answer. For example: "This service runs in 32 production clusters and one ops cluster. Should each cluster be judged on its own?"Starts from what your team knows. It mines your alert rules and dashboards first, since they encode failure modes, thresholds, and severities your team already agreed on.Measures normal over time. It checks each signal at several points over the past week and reads daily and weekly traffic cycles, so a quiet Sunday night doesn't look like an outage.Validates and writes it all down. Every check is tested against live data before it's saved, along with a calibration context: a compact decision guide covering the service, your decisions, deploy behavior, normal ranges, and known noise.A calibration takes a few minutes at most. Call for call, it's the most expensive thing a watcher does, but it happens once, not every 10 minutes.Run plain code, then make one model callA calibrated watcher doesn't explore anything at run time. It executes its saved checks and turns the results into a compact digest, without a model:Metrics: Code compares each value with the same time yesterday and with a statistical baseline, then applies the calibrated thresholds, so the model gets verdicts it can't miscompute.Logs: Loki's patterns API already groups log lines into patterns at ingestion. The watcher keeps an inventory of them across runs, so it can spot new patterns, notice when a known one doubles in rate, and fetch examples only for what's new.Deploys: A check that reports rollouts lets the model tell "this started right after a deploy" from coincidence.Healthy checks collapse to one line each, and the digest goes to exactly one model call, with no tools. The model returns a structured decision: an assessment (OK, warning, or critical), a short report, the issues it's tracking and their evidence, and whether to notify anyone or launch an investigation.For example, let's say you roll out a deployment and five minutes later you get an error rate that's slightly up and a log pattern nobody has seen before. Is that noise, or is it worth waking someone up for? This is a task that LLMs are genuinely good at. Weighing evidence like that and explaining the call plays to an LLM's strengths while crunching thousands of data points doesn't. Because the question is this narrow, a small, fast model is enough.We don't take that on faith, either. Our evals replay real production decisions against candidate models, and the model most watchers use today didn't miss a single critical case, at about half the cost per decision of the model it replaced.What it costsHere's what that adds up to for the 43 Watchers running on our internal stack, at our list price of $2 per million tokens:Types of WatchersCost to run per monthMedian WatcherLess than $541 of 43 WatchersLess than $10Most expensive Watcher (43 checks, every 15 minutes)A little over $20Even the most expensive one spends less than one cent per run. Cost follows the two things you control: how often a watcher runs (every five minutes to every three hours) and how much it watches. Calibration comes on top, and investigations a watcher launches are billed as investigations. Each watcher's Overview tab estimates its monthly token usage, so you see the cost before your bill does.Watchers are free until Dec. 1, 2026. After that, they will draw on your plan’s monthly system-initiated allowance (shared with other automated work) and bill on Assistant token usage. See Grafana Assistant pricing for more info.Note: Watchers will work exactly as they do today when billing goes live, and we expect the cost of running one to remain in line with what we’ve shared here.What our own watcher foundA cost-effective watcher is only worth it if it catches things. Over the past few months, the watcher our team runs on Grafana Assistant itself found more than 10 production bugs that affected customers, including:A crashlooping Microsoft Teams integrationBroken investigation reportsMissing webhook credentials in a newly enabled regionSlack OAuth failuresEven bugs in Watchers themselves, like alerts that never reached AlertmanagerMany of these surfaced as a new error pattern in the logs. A new pattern alone is often noise, but one that lines up with rising errors and a fresh deploy usually isn't. That's exactly the kind of call a watcher makes well.It isn't always right about the cause, and it doesn't need to be. During one rollout, it flagged real failures from an exhausted MySQL database but blamed the wrong cause, and engineers found an expensive query plan that likely contributed. The watcher notices; people, or an Assistant Investigation, dig in.Plug it into your stackA watcher can sit on top of most of your stack:Data sources: Prometheus (including Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus), CloudWatch metrics, Loki, Tempo, Pyroscope, Synthetic Monitoring, Grafana-managed alerts, and BigQuery for business signals. With the Infinity data source, it can also read any HTTP API that returns JSON or XML. One of ours watches the status pages of the LLM providers that Assistant depends on.Destinations: Slack, Microsoft Teams, signed webhooks, and Grafana Alerting, so findings flow through your notification policies and contact points, including Grafana Cloud IRM. A critical finding can also launch an Assistant Investigation or trigger an Assistant Automation.Watchers don't replace alert rules; they cover what you can't spell out in advance. To find the right mix, ask Assistant to review a service, and it recommends an alert, a watcher, or both for each failure mode.To try it, go to AI > Watchers in Grafana Cloud and create a watcher for a service your team checks by hand after every release. Describe what normal looks like, pick your data sources, and let calibration do the rest. To learn more, refer to the Watchers documentation.

title: Only include resource detectors you need by building your own Collector
description:
There are many reasons for building your own OpenTelemetry Collector
distribution. The existing distributions are designed to be broadly useful,
which means they include many more components than what an individual deployment
uses. Building your own gives you the ability to select only the components you
care about, add your own custom components, and control exactly what ends up in
the binary you run in production.
One of the reasons I prefer to build my own distribution is to limit the size of
the binary I have to ship around and to ensure that the least amount of
dependencies are included. Fewer dependencies means a smaller binary, a smaller
attack surface, and fewer third-party modules to track when a vulnerability is
disclosed. The
OpenTelemetry Collector Builder (ocb) makes this
possible: you write a manifest file in YAML to select the components you care
about, and ocb compiles them into the resulting binary.

Bridging Alloy and OpenTelemetry: the OTel engine is now in Public Preview
description:
Many Grafana Cloud customers love what Alloy offers them, but we're also seeing a growing base of users who feel the same way about the OpenTelemetry Collector. We want to make it easy for customers to make the decision that makes the most sense, regardless of their preference.When we introduced the OpenTelemetry engine for Grafana Alloy, we set out to give teams a way to run native OTLP pipelines without giving up the power and flexibility Alloy is known for. Since then we've kept building: ironing out service installation support, enabling Fleet Management, and folding in feedback from early users. Today, as of Alloy v1.21.0, we're happy to share that the OTel engine has moved into Public Preview, running right alongside the default engine you already know. In this post, we'll dig into when you'd reach for each engine, walk through some of the most interesting use cases we've seen so far, and give a preview of where both engines are headed next.The motivation behind each engineBefore diving into specific new features, let’s recap why we have two engines in Alloy.Default engineThe default engine is a cross-ecosystem engine at its core; it's not tied to any single wire format or vendor. It can just as easily run a Prometheus pipeline, an OTLP pipeline, or a Loki pipeline, all defined using Alloy's own configuration syntax. That flexibility is what makes it a Swiss army knife: the same engine that scrapes Prometheus metrics can pull in logs over syslog for logs, ingest OTLP, scrape Prometheus metrics from embedded exporters, and route all of it to wherever it needs to go.OpenTelemetry engine There's a lot to like about being able to speak every ecosystem's language. But the telemetry landscape itself is moving in the opposite direction. Rather than translating between formats, the industry is increasingly converging on a single, shared model defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. That's what an OpenTelemetry Collector actually is: a pipeline that treats OTLP as the native format end-to-end, prioritizing portability and open standards over ecosystem-bridging translation. At its core, Alloy's OTel engine is Grafana Labs' own distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.Running the OTel engineIt's just a collector The OTel engine is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution that ships inside Alloy. It runs standard collector YAML with no translation and no Alloy syntax. If you already have a collector config, you already have an OTel engine config.- otelcol --config=config.yaml
+ alloy otel --config=config.yamlThe rest of the CLI matches, too. validate, components, print-config, and --set all work the way they do upstream, so scripts and CI that call otelcol validate keep working.The same goes for the tools you deploy collectors with. On the upstream Helm chart, it's two values:image:
  repository: grafana/alloy
command:
  name: "bin/otelcol"The OpenTelemetry Operator used to fail on the Alloy image because it had no way to set the container command. We added spec.command upstream (Operator v0.153.0 and later), so now it's one line:spec:
  image: grafana/alloy:<ALLOY_VERSION>
  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]For a non-containerized installation, the Alloy packages can run either engine as a service. Set ALLOY_OTEL_MODE=1 and the service runs the OTel engine against config.yaml. Read our docs for more information on how to set it up by platform.Fleet management Managing collector configuration by hand doesn't scale past a handful of hosts, so remote configuration was one of the first gaps we closed after the initial release. As of Alloy v1.19.0, you can manage OTel engine configuration centrally with Fleet Management. The OpAMP supervisor is embedded in the Alloy binary and runs through the new experimental otel-supervisor subcommand: point it at your Fleet Management endpoint and credentials with a supervisor configuration file, and Alloy handles the connection, pulls down your pipeline configuration, and applies changes as you publish them. See the Alloy otel-supervisor reference to get started.An escape hatch: the alloyengine extensionSometimes the component you need only exists in the default engine today. The alloyengine extension runs Alloy configuration inside the same collector process, so you can pick up that one piece without running a second agent.It's Experimental, and we expect it to stay that way. The two engines run side by side but can't pass data to each other directly, so anything that crosses over goes out over the network, usually OTLP.If you reach for it, tell us why. Open an issue on the Alloy repo with the component you needed. That list is how we decide which default engine pieces become native OpenTelemetry collector components next.Experiments with Grafana Cloud productsHeads up first: nothing in this section is supported, and you shouldn't run it in production. Part of what we're working out with the OTel engine is how Grafana Cloud's products behave when the pipeline is OTel end to end. Here's where two of them stand.Database Observability. Today the path that works is adding your existing Alloy config to the collector you already run. Your OTLP pipelines keep doing their thing, and the extension runs database observability next to them. The Database Observability app can't tell the difference:extensions:
  alloyengine:
    config:
      inline:
        content: |
          database_observability.postgres "default" {
            data_source_name = env("POSTGRES_DSN")
            forward_to       = [loki.write.grafana_cloud.receiver]
          }
          // ...the rest of your existing Alloy config

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
      http: {}

service:
  extensions: [alloyengine]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp_http/grafana_cloud]A native collector path is in the works but still further off as we decide how to break the Alloy components out into OpenTelemetry native ones.Cloud Provider Observability. Alloy's cloud provider exporters, like prometheus.exporter.gcp, work through the extension the same way. The data will be identical when run in the alloyengine extension as when run in Alloy’s default engine. The more interesting result is what happens without Alloy’s native Prometheus exporters at all. We've been working with the Prometheus community to make exporters embeddable as libraries, so they run as real collector receivers instead of something a collector scrapes. With a collector built to include it, the GCP exporter is just another receiver:receivers:
  stackdriver_exporter:
    exporter_config:
      project_ids: ["<PROJECT_ID>"]
      metrics_prefixes: [compute.googleapis.com/instance]
      aggregate_deltas: true  # off by default; Alloy turns it onLooking beyond Cloud Provider Observability, the OpenTelemetry Collector Prometheus Distro is an official, experimental collector distribution that ships embeddable Prometheus exporters as OpenTelemetry receivers including blackbox, Postgres, Google Cloud Monitoring with stackdriver exporter and CloudWatch through yet-another-cloudwatch exporter. The receivers live in prometheus-opentelemetry-collector if you'd rather build your own with Open Telemetry Collector Builder (OCB). As they progress through the OpenTelemetry stability model we will look to add them to the OTel engine.Looking aheadOTel engine So what comes next for the OTel engine now that it's in Public Preview? Making sure you can properly debug your collector is high on the list. Support bundles are a key feature for this in the default engine —a single request to /-/support packages your configuration, logs, internal metrics, runtime flags, and pprof profiles into one file you can inspect before sharing. The OTel engine has no equivalent today, so we're building an OTel-native extension to match it. Stay tuned for more updates on that front!We also want to hear what's pulling you back to the default engine via the Alloy engine extension. The extension is there as an escape hatch, but we plan to break those pieces out into native collector components, the way we've started with Prometheus exporters. If you've reached for the extension, or held off on the OTel engine because something was missing, tell us what it was.Default engineThe default engine isn't standing still. Most of the work ahead is about one thing: making sure your data always arrives, even when something downstream is having a bad day.Prometheus: a better Remote Write Today  prometheus.remote_write is what keeps your metrics from disappearing when your backend goes down, and there’s a lot going on to improve it:Smaller footprint. Keeping what’s in memory and what’s on disk as small as possible to help in high scale environments and keep restart delays minimal.Pickup where you left off. Data that was in flight when Alloy restarted should still get sent.Remote Write 2.0. When we moved our own internal Prometheus workloads to it, egress costs for that telemetry dropped by more than half. You can try it in prometheus.remote_write today as an experimental feature, and we're helping push it toward stable upstream.Because prometheus.remote_write builds on upstream Prometheus, much of this work happens upstream, so it helps the whole Prometheus ecosystem, not just Alloy.Loki: pipelines that know when something failedAlloy's log pipelines still use a design inherited from Promtail, where components pass logs with no way to report back whether delivery worked. That's behind most of the rough edges you might have experienced: logs lost when Alloy shuts down, a slow stage holding up everything behind it, and file positions that advance before a line is actually sent. We're rebuilding the pipeline so success and failure flow back to the source:No silent gaps. A file's position only moves once its lines are delivered, and Alloy drains in-flight logs on shutdown instead of dropping them.Throughput that scales. A slow stage stops blocking the whole pipeline, so giving Alloy more CPU actually buys you more throughput.A WAL you can rely on. We're working through the known issues to take the loki.write WAL to general availability, so logs survive an outage or a restart on disk.Both engines are shaped by what we hear from the people running them, so tell us what you want us to focus on next. Open an issue on the Alloy repo or come find us in #alloy on the Grafana Community Slack.

title: Trace linkage: connect the dots between your app traces and database queries
description: When an application request slows down, a trace can show a database call. Finding the database query behind it can be tedious, requiring you to switch between traces and database telemetry, as well as match timestamps or query text by hand. In Grafana Cloud, the Database Observability app already provides a window into all of your database telemetry, including query samples, performance history, and explain plan. But what if you could jump from that database call in the trace straight to its query details?OpenTelemetry database semantic conventions stabilized last year, giving us all a dependable shared language for describing database operations. That foundation has opened the door for what we call trace linkage, now Generally Available in Database Observability!What is trace linkage?With trace linkage, we try to provide a connection between OpenTelemetry-instrumented applications and database telemetry collected with Alloy. In other words, when you give us these previously-disjoint puzzle pieces, we’ll do our best to provide you as much supporting information between these two elements as we can. And we'll do it without making you tediously piece together timestamps and logs. From a database span in a trace, you’ll see a link on the query text. Clicking from there, the app searches for a connection between your database query and our opinionated view of your most relevant data in the Database Observability app. You can explore sampled query execution data or check out the query’s historical performance, alongside that query’s related schema and explain plan.This connection builds on the database attributes your OpenTelemetry instrumentation already emits. Grafana Cloud Traces, powered by Tempo, retain those attributes, and trace linkage uses the query text, database system, and database name to connect a database span to its supporting query context in Database Observability. We support the stable conventions like db.query.text and its legacy equivalent db.statement, so existing instrumentation can continue to benefit as teams adopt the stable conventions.How does it work?The initial idea for trace linkage came from this question: What shared context could connect application instrumentation with telemetry collected from the database?The answer was to leverage trace context: the trace ID and span ID. On one side we have an application trace with spans representing a query execution. On the Database Observability side, we are collecting telemetry from the database concerning query executions. As long as the telemetry we collect contains the same trace ID and span ID, we can make a link between the application trace and Database Observability. This led us to sqlcommenter, an open source project donated to the OpenTelemetry community. Its idea is (delightfully) simple: let the SQL statement carry a piece of trace context with it in a comment. With trace context propagation enabled, sqlcommenter injects the application’s trace ID and span ID into a comment at the end of the SQL statement. This is done at the level of an individual query execution, so this is like a shared thread that allows us to follow from a trace span to a specific query execution.We then search the trace ID and span ID in the logs that we generated in the Database Observability Alloy component: our component extracts traceparent from the SQL comment and includes it in query sample logs.Going beyond a traceparent matchHowever, having sqlcommenter enabled doesn’t guarantee that Alloy captured the particular SQL execution. That can depend on how short-lived a query may be or how often Alloy polls the database. Even if you are ready to use sqlcommenter, not every database engine is supported, and it can come with downsides for database caches. This means that you might have traces for which we can’t find a query sample in Database Observability, at least not with  sqlcommenter exclusively.We can go beyond sqlcommenter-based matching by using the query statement itself. When we can’t find an exact match, we look for matching query text in the telemetry collected by Alloy.That sounds straightforward, but the same query can look different on each side. OpenTelemetry instrumentation doesn’t always record statements in the same way: depending on the language and instrumentation used, literal values may be preserved or masked, and parameter placeholders can take different forms. Meanwhile, database engines apply their own normalization to the query text that Alloy collects. We account for these differences, along with formatting and comments, to find a match.Even when we can’t point you to the exact execution, you can still explore the samples and historical performance we’ve gathered for that query! This lets us make a meaningful link between your traces and Database Observability, even without sqlcommenter.Start with query text matching, then use sqlcommenter to match trace and span IDs exactlyTrace linkage can be a great tool for quickly connecting your database and application telemetry, so we're excited for you to try it today. If your application is already instrumented as an OpenTelemetry SDK that sends traces to Grafana Cloud and you’ve already set up Database Observability, then read our docs about setting up trace linkage to help you get started. If Database Observability has collected a query and the database span already includes its text in db.query.text or the legacy db.statement, chances are trace linkage can already match the span to that query without further application instrumentation.Once you’ve tried query text matching, you can optionally go beyond and match a trace to a specific query execution with the use of sqlcommenter, as this blog discussed extensively. This improves match precision; exact matches remain best-effort because Alloy may not sample that execution.And if you aren't sure where to start, ask Grafana Assistant for help, using natural language.

title: Instrumentation Hub in Grafana Cloud: start easier, stay in control
description: It's no secret that getting started with observability can be much harder than it should be. That's why, at ObservabilityCon 2025, we introduced Instrumentation Hub: a guided, scalable way to roll out observability coverage while still keeping you in control. Today, we’re excited to announce that Instrumentation Hub is now Generally Available in Grafana Cloud.As we hinted at before, this new iteration introduces selective OpenTelemetry SDK injection, giving you deeper runtime insights for a wide range of languages to complement eBPF instrumentation with a single click. What is the Instrumentation Hub?Instrumentation Hub makes the biggest bottleneck of starting with observability, instrumentation, faster and easier by leveraging open source eBPF and OTel injection.At Grafana Labs, we're champions of open-standards-based observability, but we also realize that getting meaningful coverage of your systems can often mean months of manual toil. Each layer requires its own instrumentation approach, balancing technology tradeoffs, and unique brittle steps. Organizational challenges exacerbate this process, making observability a moving target with uneven coverage, persistent blind spots, and ultimately leaving you wondering if the effort was worth the pain.We believe there’s a better way. Instrumentation Hub is a control plane for remote discovery and selective auto-instrumentation. It helps you go from zero to meaningful telemetry in a matter of minutes by removing the bottleneck of having to apply instrumentation by hand.How Instrumentation Hub worksThe premise is simple: you run a single Helm command on your Kubernetes cluster to install Alloy, our distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.Once installed, Instrumentation Hub automatically catalogs everything that’s running on the cluster, structured by namespace and technology. Teams can immediately see what exists, what’s instrumented, and what isn’t.Then, you use either the Grafana Cloud UI, an API automation, or your favorite LLM agent to describe what and how you want to collect and monitor.Under the hood, Instrumentation Hub translates these selections into observability pipelines without the need for manual configuration. Within minutes you can begin exploring insights across your infrastructure and services in the Grafana Cloud observability platform.And of course, this isn’t a one-time setup. Teams can come back any time and refine their observability scope by namespace and enable or disable specific signal collection to balance their observability budgets. Need profiles for a misbehaving service? Enable them temporarily. Too many logs from a noisy workload? Exclude them. Trying to reduce spend? Dial back collection where it’s no longer needed.Observability is a progressionLast year at ObservabilityCon, we introduced the idea of a hierarchy of observability needs as a mental model to chart an effective path for applying observability. We described how you should start from a bird’s eye view of your estate and gradually move towards deeper and more customized insights.Instrumentation Hub is built around this progression, facilitating observability in the right order for a maximum return on investment.At the base is the foundation everything depends on: infrastructure visibility, which provides insight into the machines the code runs on. Instrumentation Hub helps you get started at this layer by enabling Kubernetes Monitoring with the click of a button.Above infrastructure is baseline service visibility. RED metrics and service relationships provide a consistent, system-wide view so teams can quickly triage issues and narrow the search space before digging deeper. Instrumentation Hub populates Grafana Cloud's Knowledge Graph in a matter of minutes, providing rich context for humans and agents.At the next level, technology-specific and transaction-level insights become necessary. Distributed traces reveal application behavior across the full request path, exposing performance bottlenecks and dependencies that aren’t visible from the outside.This is where Instrumentation Hub stands out. It can selectively deploy OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation SDKs with the click of a button.Historically, this process meant installing a new Operator, deploying instrumentation CRDs, annotating your target applications, and restarting the pods. This work can span across multiple teams, ownership boundaries, or require a dedicated new collection layer. But now, the very same upstream SDKs can be rolled out to complement and enrich your existing baseline service visibility without any extra moving pieces and without disruptive restarts.Get started with Instrumentation Hub todayTry it out! The Instrumentation Hub is available to all Grafana Cloud stacks for your Kubernetes clusters running on Linux.If you’ve recently installed the Kubernetes Monitoring Helm chart you might be set up with it already. And if you're still unsure, ask Grafana Assistant for help!

title: Grafana 13.3 release: manage variables across dashboards, share findings with Notebooks, a UI refresh, and more
description: Grafana 13.3 is here, bringing more consistency and control to how you work across Grafana. Cross-dashboard variables help you manage shared dashboard controls from one place, while Notebooks let you capture and share findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. You'll also get a first look at Grafana's biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, along with new ways to guide and refine dashboards built with Grafana Assistant.Below are just some of the highlights from this release. You can explore all of the updates in the changelog or our What's new in Grafana 13.3 documentation.Define a variable once and use it across dashboardsAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaWhen multiple dashboards use the same variable, such as an environment, region, or cluster selector, managing it separately in each dashboard creates duplicate work and can lead to configuration drift. To address this, we’re rolling out cross-dashboard variables, which let you define a variable once and reuse it across dashboards in your Grafana organization.You can create and manage these variables from Dashboards > Variables, and scope each one as either:Global: available to every dashboard in the organizationFolder: available only to dashboards in the same folderWhen you edit a dashboard, add a variable from the sidebar and select Global or folder variable. Grafana shows only the variables available to that dashboard's scope, and you can add them one at a time or all at once. Viewers can still change the variable's value on the dashboard, while its configuration stays managed centrally, so shared controls stay consistent without editing every dashboard that uses them.To try cross-dashboard variables in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the cross-dashboard variables documentation.Consolidate and share your findings with NotebooksAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaAn investigation rarely happens in one place. You might start on a dashboard panel, jump into Explore to run a query, and then ask Grafana Assistant what's going on. Until now, the evidence and your reasoning ended up scattered across tabs, screenshots, and chat threads.Notebooks let you capture findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. Add panels from dashboards or Explore, pull in findings from Grafana Assistant, and write your observations right next to the data. Teammates can then follow your investigation, understand how you reached your conclusions, and collaborate on next steps.You can use a notebook to:Explore a question about your data, keeping queries and notes side by side as your thinking develops.Document an investigation so the next person doesn't have to start from scratch.Prepare a post-incident review with the relevant panels already in place.You can create notebooks manually or with Grafana Assistant, then save and share them for future reference. The new Notebooks page also makes it easy to find and manage your work, with options to search, filter, edit, and export notebooks. Notebooks are gradually rolling out to Grafana Cloud. To try them in self-managed Grafana, enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the Notebooks documentation.A fresh new look for the Grafana UIAvailable in public preview in all editions of GrafanaWhether it’s adding new data sources or supporting new use cases, we’re constantly expanding what Grafana can do. And as AI-powered workflows with Grafana Assistant became a bigger part of how people use Grafana every day, we saw an opportunity to rethink how the platform looks and feels.With Grafana 13.3, we're introducing the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7. Built on an updated set of design principles, the refresh introduces new colors, typography, and UI components to create a more modern, consistent experience across Grafana.Updates include: New default dark and light themes. We've reworked every theme color, with more shades for flexibility, and main action buttons now have a solid, high-contrast style.Softer borders and floating components. Rounder corners offer a more modern feel, and subtle borders on cards, panels, and drawers create a clearer sense of depth. The toolbar and navigation also stand apart more clearly from page content.Updated inputs, drop-downs, buttons, and tags. We've resized our most-used components to be more proportional and consistent. Revised typography. A new type scale mixes font weights and sizes, rather than relying on size alone, so it's easier to see what matters most on a page. Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Your existing workflows and navigation stay the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins that use standard Grafana components and theme tokens will automatically pick up the new look, while those with custom styling can migrate on their own timeline.To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous design at any time, and we welcome your feedback as we continue rolling out improvements over the coming months.Build and edit dashboards with more control using Grafana Assistant Grafana Assistant can already help you build and edit dashboards from a plain-language description. Now, with Grafana 13.3, you have more control over that process, from reviewing and refining a dashboard plan before it's built to easily undoing changes afterward. Review a dashboard plan from AssistantAvailable in public preview in all editions of Grafana With dashboard plans, you can describe what you want to monitor, and instead of building it right away, Assistant proposes a plan in chat. The plan covers the dashboard title, tabs or rows, panels, visualization types, and variables, so you can catch a missing panel or the wrong chart type before anything is built.Select Preview to open a read-only version of the dashboard, then keep the conversation going to iterate from there. When the preview matches what you need, select Build it to generate the dashboard and save it.Quickly revert Assistant edits Generally available in all editions of Grafana Experimenting with different layouts and visualizations is easier when you can quickly undo changes you don’t want. With Grafana 13.3, you can now select Undo turn after Grafana Assistant edits your dashboard to restore it to its previous state. If Assistant changed multiple panels in a single request, you can undo all those changes at once.To learn more, refer to the Grafana Assistant dashboarding guide.More to explore in Grafana 13.3Beyond these highlights, Grafana 13.3 includes a range of updates related to data visualization, alerting, Git Sync, and more. For an in-depth list of all the new features, check out our Grafana documentation, the Grafana changelog, or our What's New documentation.Join the Grafana Labs communityWe invite you to engage with the Grafana Labs community forums. Share your experiences with the new features, discuss best practices, and explore creative ways to integrate these updates into your workflows. Your insights and use cases are invaluable in enriching the Grafana ecosystem.Upgrade to Grafana 13.3Download Grafana 13.3 today or experience all the latest features by signing up for Grafana Cloud, which offers an actually useful forever-free tier and plans for every use case. Sign up for a free Grafana Cloud account today. Our Grafana upgrade guide also provides step-by-step instructions for those looking to upgrade from an earlier version to ensure a smooth transition.Special thanks to our communityWe extend our heartfelt gratitude to the Grafana community! Your contributions, ranging from pull requests to valuable feedback, are crucial in continually enhancing Grafana. And your enthusiasm and dedication inspire us at Grafana Labs to persistently innovate and elevate the Grafana platform.

title: Bliki: LLM Voice
description:
Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading
  the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common
  tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I
  do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion

There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference
  between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary
  of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather
  misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we
  are in an uncanny
  valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm
  reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM
  present.

I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language
  changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language
  of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a
  new sales motion,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard
  these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational
  difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit,
  don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.)

Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I
  strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the
  LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel
  the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 
1
 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I
  have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that
  may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 
2

  Authors should fill the prose themselves. 

Say Your Writing is
  even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head
  and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice
  is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate
  regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies
  on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering
  to an LLM will undermine any progress.

In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the
  difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find
  writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing
  something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence.
  I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but
  the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As
  more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and
  comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then?

Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An
  important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He
  finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's
  disease. I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my
  old friend's wisdom.

A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't
  comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found
  LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who
  know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the
  smooth but soulless LLM.

There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native
  Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter
  to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 
3
. Maybe
  most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't
  have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my
  humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose.


Notes


1: 
      Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know
      the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when
      I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a
      major periodical publication to clean it up.
    



2: 
      My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write
       should declare how they used it, usually in the
      acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that
      readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI
